cues.text: Two homes, one family
In 1953, Zidane’s parents left their village in Kabylia, Algeria, and moved to Paris.
Work was hard to find, so in the 1960s they moved to La Castellane, a tough part of Marseille.
Zinedine was born there in 1972, the youngest of five children.
Open the suitcase.
His father often worked night shifts in a warehouse and as a security guard.
His parents were strict, and Zidane calls his father the guiding light of his career.
He later said he is proud of being French, and proud of his family’s roots too.
Your family’s story is part of you. Coming from two places can be a strength.
Far from home
When Zidane was fourteen, a scout from the club Cannes, Jean Varraud, spotted him at a training camp.
He went to Cannes for six weeks, and ended up staying for four years.
That meant leaving his family and sleeping in a dormitory with twenty other young players.
Knock three times on the paper door.
The club’s director, Jean-Claude Elineau, invited Zidane to leave the dormitory and live with his own family.
Zidane later said that in their home he found balance.
Being far from home is hard, and a kind grown-up can make a big difference.
Being new somewhere is hard. It’s okay to ask for help and to accept kindness.
Words that hurt
At Cannes, some spectators shouted insults about Zidane’s race and his family.
His first coaches saw that he was sensitive.
Once he punched an opponent who had mocked the neighbourhood he came from, and as a punishment he spent his first weeks cleaning.
Lift the flap to see who helped.
His coach, Jean Varraud, encouraged him to turn his anger into focus on his own game.
Some writers describe Zidane as caught between two cultures.
Unkind words about who you are are never okay, and hitting back only makes things harder.
If someone is unkind about who you are, it is not your fault. Tell someone you trust.
Sent off, then back
In 1998, France hosted the World Cup.
In France’s second match, Zidane was sent off for stamping on an opponent.
He became the first French player ever shown a red card at a World Cup, and for a while he could only watch.
Open the tunnel gate to bring him back.
His team won without him, and when he returned they kept going, all the way to the final against Brazil.
There, Zidane scored two headers, and France won 3–0.
A red card was not the end of his story.
A setback isn’t the end of the story. Your team can carry you while you’re out.
Coming back
In 2004, after France were knocked out of the European Championship by Greece, Zidane retired from playing for France.
Other older players left too, and France struggled to qualify for the 2006 World Cup.
Unfold the bridge back to the team.
The coach, Raymond Domenech, urged Zidane to return, and in 2005 he came back as captain, with his old teammates Lilian Thuram and Claude Makélélé.
Together they helped France climb from fourth place to the top of their group.
Sometimes the bravest thing is to come back and help.
It’s okay to step away. Coming back when people need you is brave too.
A hard night, and after
The 2006 World Cup final against Italy was Zidane’s last match.
He scored a penalty, but in extra time a player insulted his sister, and Zidane pushed his head into the player’s chest.
He was sent off, and France lost on penalties.
Clear the storm cloud.
Back in Paris, thousands of fans still cheered his name.
Zidane later said twelve of his fourteen red cards came after someone provoked him, but that this was no excuse.
Later, as Real Madrid’s coach, he won the Champions League three years in a row.
When someone tries to make you angry, breathe and walk away. You are more than one bad moment.
